title: Jelly kept her from his friends; the Little Jelly nickname
summary: He came alone to see her, treated her as still sixteen, and refused to let friends call her Little Jelly.

story.theme_name: Chicago: the jazz migration and its clubs
story.community_name: Going north: working the Chicago jazz scene

blocks.x: Do you remember anybody else coming to the house that he played with? Any other musicians? I would have done. No. Tony Jackson was dead at that time.

But, Jelly, you listen here, he would come alone to pick me up. He'd come and visit me alone. He'd ever bring any of his friends around. And he would always, he'd give me some kind of excuse when I said, well, tomorrow we're going downtown, may I stop over there? And he said, no, baby, I'll let you know when you can come. And he always wanted to treat me like I was still 16, you know. You just couldn't imagine I was married and had a child. But I told him one time, I said, I'd never been to Dry Street until I got ready to come up here. I went to Dry Street to buy my suitcase. He said, Dry Street? Just started off Canal Street. I said, yeah, but the stores are way up in the 1700 block. And I was afraid to go up that far. 1700 block from Canal Street. And I was afraid to go up there. But the raised girls were so timid in those days. I mean, they aren't timid now. You hear these little 10-year-old say some things that shock you.

Well, there were some of the musicians around Chicago that I've talked to, like Maddie Dominick and Roy Palmer, a trombonist. Mm-hmm. And Lee Collins, who's now dead, a coronet player. They made records with your brother. With Jelly, yes. Around that time, 1924 and 23.

And then, you see, his friends wanted to call me Little Jelly, and he didn't want that. He'd say, her name's Mimi. And you see, they wouldn't think of my name. They'd say, all right, Little Jelly, so-and-so. And he kept me away from his friends. He didn't want me to be nicknamed Little Jelly. No. Was he much taller? He didn't seem much taller than you. He's six feet three. Six feet three. Yes, sir. He's taller than my tallest uncle. This isn't very good of him either. No, no. He was six feet old.
